title: Pathophysiology: Potassium Disorders—Cellular Shifts, Dysrhythmias and Safe Correction
html:
Potassium is the major intracellular cation, while only a small fraction is present in extracellular fluid. That small extracellular concentration strongly influences nerve conduction, skeletal-muscle function, and cardiac electrical activity. A serum potassium result can change because potassium was gained or lost from the body, shifted between cells and extracellular fluid, or was measured inaccurately. The RN connects the value to symptoms, ECG, kidney function, acid–base status, glucose and insulin, medications, urine output, tissue injury, and the speed of change.

Learning goals

  • Explain intracellular and extracellular potassium balance.
  • Distinguish true potassium gain or loss from transcellular shifts and specimen error.
  • Identify common mechanisms of hypokalemia and hyperkalemia.
  • Recognize neuromuscular, gastrointestinal, and cardiac manifestations.
  • Interpret ECG findings as variable risk cues rather than perfect diagnostic stages.
  • Apply safety principles for oral and intravenous potassium replacement.
  • Differentiate cardiac stabilization, temporary intracellular shifting, and potassium removal in hyperkalemia treatment.
  • Evaluate response using serial potassium, glucose, ECG, symptoms, renal function, and ongoing losses.

Serum potassium is a small window into a large store

Most potassium is inside cells. The sodium–potassium ATPase maintains the gradient by moving potassium into cells and sodium out. Because extracellular potassium represents only a small portion of total-body potassium, a rapid transcellular shift can substantially change the serum value without an equivalent gain or loss from the body. Conversely, a client may have a significant total-body deficit even after the serum value temporarily normalizes during replacement.

Internal balance shifts potassium between cells and extracellular fluid over minutes to hours. External balance depends mainly on renal excretion, with smaller gastrointestinal losses. The kidneys adapt potassium excretion through distal sodium delivery, tubular flow, aldosterone activity, acid–base state, and kidney function.

Insulin, beta-adrenergic activity, and acid–base status shift potassium

Insulin activates cellular potassium uptake. Beta-2 adrenergic stimulation also shifts potassium into cells. These mechanisms help buffer potassium after meals and are used therapeutically in selected hyperkalemic emergencies. Alkalemia often favors movement into cells, while mineral acidosis can favor movement outward, but the relationship is not uniform across all acid–base disorders.

Cell destruction from rhabdomyolysis, burns, tumor lysis, hemolysis, or severe tissue injury can release intracellular potassium. Insulin deficiency and hyperosmolality can shift potassium outward even when total-body potassium is depleted, as may occur in diabetic ketoacidosis. Treat the mechanism, not an isolated assumption about direction.

A normalizing serum value may hide ongoing risk
When treatment shifts potassium into cells, it does not remove potassium from the body. When insulin therapy moves potassium into cells, an initially elevated value can fall rapidly despite a total-body deficit. Continue ordered surveillance after the first improved result.

Hypokalemia: loss, shift, or inadequate intake

Hypokalemia commonly results from gastrointestinal loss, renal loss, or movement into cells. Diarrhea and gastrointestinal drainage can directly remove potassium. Vomiting more often promotes renal potassium loss through volume depletion, aldosterone activity, chloride depletion, and alkalosis rather than by losing large amounts of potassium in vomitus. Loop and thiazide diuretics, mineralocorticoid excess, some renal tubular disorders, and medications can increase urinary loss.

Insulin, beta-agonists, alkalemia, and rapid production of new cells can shift potassium inward. Low intake alone is less often the only cause, but it worsens loss. Low magnesium can increase renal potassium wasting and make hypokalemia difficult to correct, so magnesium should be evaluated when replacement is ineffective or risk is high.

Low potassium impairs excitable tissues

Cues may include fatigue, muscle weakness, cramps, reduced reflexes, constipation, ileus, palpitations, or respiratory-muscle weakness. Severe or rapidly developing hypokalemia can cause paralysis and life-threatening dysrhythmias. Risk is greater with heart disease, ischemia, digoxin exposure, other electrolyte abnormalities, and medications that prolong repolarization.

Possible ECG findings include T-wave flattening, ST depression, prominent U waves, apparent QT or QU prolongation, ectopy, and atrial or ventricular dysrhythmias. The pattern varies, and classic changes may be absent. The RN treats the client, confirmed result, trend, symptoms, and rhythm—not a memorized ECG sequence alone.

Confirm the mechanism and identify ongoing losses

Review vomiting, diarrhea, drains, nutrition, insulin, beta-agonists, diuretics, laxatives, corticosteroid or mineralocorticoid effects, and recent treatment. Assess muscle strength, bowel function, breathing, pulse and rhythm. Review magnesium, glucose, acid–base status, kidney function, and urine potassium studies when ordered.

A low serum value caused mainly by an intracellular shift may respond differently from a large total-body deficit. Ongoing gastrointestinal or renal loss can defeat replacement. Document the timing of replacement and repeat testing so the result can be interpreted accurately.

Potassium replacement is high-alert therapy

Oral replacement is often preferred when the situation and gastrointestinal function permit because absorption is slower. Oral products can irritate the gastrointestinal tract and must be given in the correct formulation; extended-release products should not be crushed unless the product and order allow it. Follow food, dilution, and tube-administration instructions for the specific product.

Intravenous potassium is reserved for appropriate indications and must be diluted, administered by an infusion pump, and given at the ordered concentration and rate through a suitable line. Never administer IV potassium by direct IV push or undiluted injection. Verify the product, dose, dilution, route, access, pump programming, renal function, urine output, ECG-monitoring requirements, and repeat laboratory schedule according to policy. Assess the site frequently because pain, phlebitis, infiltration, and tissue injury can occur.

Stop before replacing potassium blindly
Unexpected oliguria, acute kidney injury, a rapidly changing value, new dysrhythmia, or a discrepancy between the order and current result requires clarification. A replacement order based on an old laboratory result can cause dangerous hyperkalemia.

Hyperkalemia: impaired excretion, release, shift, or excess

Reduced kidney excretion is a major cause of hyperkalemia. Risk increases with acute or chronic kidney dysfunction, reduced distal sodium delivery, low aldosterone effect, adrenal insufficiency, and combinations of medications that impair potassium excretion. Potassium supplements, salt substitutes, transfusion, and excessive administration can contribute when excretion is limited.

Cellular release occurs with tissue breakdown and hemolysis. Insulin deficiency, hyperosmolality, and some acid–base disorders shift potassium outward. Medication review includes renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system inhibitors, potassium-sparing diuretics, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, trimethoprim, heparin, and other agents relevant to the client.

Exclude pseudohyperkalemia without delaying rescue

Hemolysis during collection, prolonged tourniquet use, repeated fist clenching, delayed processing, or markedly high blood-cell counts can produce a falsely elevated result. If the client is stable and the result conflicts with the clinical picture, promptly notify the appropriate clinician and obtain a correctly collected repeat specimen as ordered.

Do not assume artifact when the value is markedly elevated, rising, accompanied by weakness or ECG change, or occurs in a high-risk client. Start cardiac monitoring and emergency assessment while confirmation proceeds according to protocol. A nonhemolyzed repeat does not erase the need to identify the cause.

High potassium can rapidly destabilize the heart

Hyperkalemia may cause paresthesias, weakness, flaccid paralysis, nausea, palpitations, bradycardia, conduction delay, ventricular dysrhythmia, or cardiac arrest. ECG changes can include peaked T waves, PR prolongation, P-wave loss, QRS widening, and merging toward a sine-wave pattern, but findings do not always progress in order and the ECG may appear deceptively normal.

Urgency depends on the potassium level and trend, symptoms, ECG, rate of rise, kidney function, and ongoing potassium release. A client with new weakness, conduction change, wide QRS, severe bradycardia, or ventricular dysrhythmia needs immediate emergency treatment.

Emergency treatment has three different jobs

Protect the myocardium: Prescribed intravenous calcium stabilizes cardiac membranes when hyperkalemia causes ECG toxicity, but it does not lower serum potassium. Continue ECG monitoring because its protective effect is temporary.

Shift potassium into cells: Prescribed insulin with glucose and beta-2 agonist therapy can temporarily lower extracellular potassium. Glucose requires repeated monitoring because insulin-related hypoglycemia may occur after the potassium result improves. Bicarbonate has a selective role when significant metabolic acidosis is present and is not a universal substitute for other therapies.

Remove potassium from the body: Definitive control may require renal excretion, gastrointestinal potassium binders, stopping sources, or dialysis, depending on severity and kidney function. Shifting alone can be followed by rebound as the temporary effect fades.

Evaluate the whole response

After hypokalemia treatment, reassess strength, respiratory function, bowel activity, rhythm, IV site, serum potassium and magnesium, kidney function, urine output, and continuing losses. Avoid assuming that one normal value means the deficit is fully restored.

After hyperkalemia treatment, reassess ECG and rhythm continuously as indicated, serial potassium, glucose after insulin, respiratory and neuromuscular function, kidney function, urine output, and whether potassium was actually removed. Report recurrent ECG change, rebound potassium, hypoglycemia, worsening weakness, oliguria, or treatment complications immediately.

Translate potassium disorders into clinical judgment

  1. Recognize cues: Identify weakness, paralysis, bowel change, palpitations, rhythm findings, kidney function, urine output, losses, tissue injury, medications, glucose, magnesium, and acid–base context.
  2. Analyze cues: Decide whether the result reflects body gain or loss, a cellular shift, impaired excretion, ongoing loss, or specimen artifact.
  3. Prioritize hypotheses: Dysrhythmia, ECG toxicity, respiratory-muscle weakness, severe symptoms, and rapidly changing potassium outrank routine teaching.
  4. Generate solutions: Plan cardiac monitoring, safe replacement, membrane stabilization, temporary shifting, definitive removal, glucose monitoring, cause correction, and serial testing as ordered.
  5. Take action: Activate emergency care when indicated, verify high-alert medications and infusions, protect the IV site, and use closed-loop communication.
  6. Evaluate outcomes: Reassess symptoms, ECG, potassium trajectory, magnesium, glucose, kidney function, urine output, ongoing loss, rebound, and adverse effects.

Clinical example

A client with acute kidney injury who takes a potassium supplement develops weakness. The laboratory reports a critically high potassium, and the ECG shows new QRS widening. The RN does not wait for a textbook sequence of changes. The RN assesses ABCs, activates the emergency pathway, starts continuous monitoring, stops potassium sources according to protocol, verifies and administers prescribed membrane-stabilizing and shifting therapies, monitors glucose, prepares for definitive removal, and evaluates serial potassium and ECG response.

Potassium disorders and high-alert therapies require client-specific diagnosis, current orders, serial laboratory and ECG monitoring, organizational protocols, pharmacy safeguards, and qualified clinical supervision. This lesson is not medical advice or clinical decision support.
